reels.title: The torn-out page

beats.say: Why does the warehouse say Meridian sold more than the app does, every single day?

show.sub: Warehouse total is higher than the app total

beats.say: Picture a shop manager with a ledger. Every night a helper photocopies only the pages with a fresh sticky note, and files the copies at head office.
Now a page is torn out because it was a test order. There is no sticky note on a missing page. The helper never notices, so head office keeps the old copy for ever.

chip.text: Deleted order stays in the warehouse

beats.say: That is timestamp polling. It finds changes it can see, but not things that vanish. Reading the shop's own diary of every action fixes it.

show.text: Read the diary, not the pages

check.q: Why does a deleted test order stay in the warehouse under timestamp polling?
opts: The warehouse refuses deletes
The deleted row no longer exists to show a newer timestamp
The job runs too slowly
Test orders have no ID
check.why: Polling selects rows that exist and changed. A deleted row is gone, so nothing tells the job to remove its copy.

work: Ask which of your pipelines copy tables by a changed-since timestamp.
Check whether any of those source tables ever have rows deleted.

reels.title: Four ways to copy a changing table

beats.say: Four ways to copy a table that keeps changing. Which one misses nothing, and at what price?

Full extract copies every row each night. With ten million orders, that is ten million rows moved even if only five thousand changed. Safe, but cost grows with the table, and in-between states are lost.
Timestamp polling asks for rows where updated at is later than the last run. It is cheap, but a deleted row has no timestamp left to find.

Triggers write each change into an audit table. Nothing is missed, but every order write now does extra work. Log-based capture reads the transaction log, the record Postgres already keeps for recovery. Nothing missed, and almost no load on the source.

check.q: What is the main cost of using triggers to capture changes?
opts: They miss deleted rows
Every write to the source table becomes slower
They need a full table copy
They lose commit order in the log
check.why: A trigger runs inside each write, adding work to the source database. It does capture deletes.

work: Write down for each source table how many rows change per day versus total rows.
Compare the cost of a full extract with changed-only copying for your largest table.

reels.title: Four blind spots of polling

beats.say: Your nightly job ran perfectly, so why is the total still wrong?
Polling has four blind spots. Hard deletes leave no row to find. An order paid, prepared and delivered between two runs shows only its final state, so the history is gone.

show.title: Blind spots, part one
items: Hard deletes leave nothing to select
Intermediate states between runs are lost

beats.say: Third, code that forgets to set updated at, such as a manual fix, is never picked up. Fourth, a slow transaction can commit late carrying an earlier timestamp. The job has already moved past that time, so the row is skipped for ever.

show.title: Blind spots, part two
items: updated_at not set, so the row looks unchanged
Late commit with an early timestamp is skipped

beats.say: Log capture sees every insert, update and delete in commit order, so none of these gaps exist.

check.q: A slow transaction commits at 02:05 but carries updated_at of 01:55. The poll last ran at 02:00. What happens?
opts: It is picked up next run
It is skipped, since its timestamp is before the last run time
It is picked up twice
The database rejects it
check.why: The next poll asks for updated_at after 02:00. The row's 01:55 value fails that test, so it is missed for good.

work: Add a daily row-count and sum reconciliation between source and warehouse.
If you must poll, overlap the window and deduplicate by key.

reels.title: When log capture is not the answer

beats.say: If log capture misses nothing, why not use it everywhere?
Because it adds parts to run: a connector, a message broker, and a replication slot on Postgres. If the consumer stalls, the slot keeps log files and can fill the source disk.

chip.text: Stalled consumer fills the source disk

beats.say: For a small table that is rarely deleted, a nightly full extract is simpler and cheaper. Triggers suit a database with no log access, if writes are light.

show.title: Simpler choices
items: Small table, few deletes: full extract
No log access, light writes: triggers

beats.say: For Meridian, with deletes, refunds and a finance audit, choose log capture, and alert on slot lag.

check.q: Which case best justifies a simple nightly full extract over log capture?
opts: A huge orders table with constant deletes
A small reference table of 2,000 rows that rarely changes
A finance audit needing every state change
A table needing sub-second freshness
check.why: A tiny, slow-changing table makes a full copy cheap, and it avoids operating a connector, broker and slot.

work: Set an alert on replication slot lag and retained log size before enabling CDC.
Classify each source table: needs deletes and history, or a full copy is enough.

reels.title: The whiteboard and the sticky notes

beats.say: How do you keep a whiteboard correct when the updates arrive messy, late, or twice?

show.sub: and the board must still be right

beats.say: The topic is a stack of sticky notes. Each note says something like, order seven is now shipped. The table is the whiteboard. It shows only where every order stands today.

Three notes about order seven in one pile? Only the newest matters, so read the numbers and use the highest. An old note turns up again? Compare its number with the one on the board, and ignore it if it is older.

show.title: Two habits
items: Many notes, one key: keep the highest number
Old note returns: skip it if the board is newer

beats.say: Follow both habits, and reading the same pile twice changes nothing. Also keep every note in a box, so you can rewrite the whole board whenever you need.

show.sub: keep the box of notes to rebuild

check.q: An old sticky note about an order arrives after a newer one was already applied. What should happen?
opts: Overwrite the board with it
Ignore it because its number is lower
Throw away the whole board
check.why: The sequence number shows the note is older than what the board holds, so applying it would roll the order back to a stale state.

work: Find one table in your lake that is fed by a changelog and name its ordering column.
Ask whether replaying yesterday's events there would change today's data.

reels.title: Four rules for applying a changelog

beats.say: A batch holds three changes to order forty-two. What happens if you merge them all at once?
A merge needs one source row per target row. Otherwise it fails, or picks one at random. So rank rows per key by log sequence number, the LSN, and keep rank one. Three changes become one.
Next, the guard. The target row stores its own LSN, say nine hundred. An incoming change with LSN eight fifty is a replay, so the update is skipped. Only a higher number wins.
Deletes need a rule too. Either remove the row, or flag it deleted so downstream models can see it. Follow all the rules, and applying the same batch twice changes nothing. That is idempotent.

show.title: Rules 3 and 4
items: Delete: remove the row, or set is_deleted true

check.q: Why must a batch be reduced to the latest change per key before a MERGE?
opts: It makes the batch smaller on disk
MERGE with several source rows per target row can fail or pick arbitrarily
It lets you skip the LSN guard
check.why: Multiple matches for one target row are ambiguous. Keeping the highest LSN per key makes the match unique and deterministic.

work: Check that your merge source is unique on the business key.
Add a stored LSN or version column to the target if it lacks one.

reels.title: The ghost row after a delete

beats.say: Your merge deletes order forty-two at LSN nine hundred. Then a replayed insert at LSN seven hundred arrives. Does the order come back?
It can. A hard delete removes the row, and its LSN goes with it. The old insert finds no match, so the not matched branch inserts it. A ghost row is back.
Fixes: soft delete and keep the LSN on the row, or keep a tombstone table of deleted keys with their LSNs, and check it before inserting.

show.title: Two fixes
items: Soft delete: is_deleted true, LSN kept

beats.say: Another trap: LSNs are only comparable within one source log. Across sources or partitions, ordering by them is wrong. And many tiny merges leave many small files, so schedule compaction.

show.title: More gotchas
items: LSN order holds within one log only

check.q: Why can a hard delete let a stale insert resurrect a row?
opts: The delete also wipes the bronze table
The LSN guard needs a matched row, and the deleted row no longer exists to compare
MERGE cannot run after a delete
check.why: The guard compares incoming LSN with the stored LSN. With no row, the insert branch fires with nothing to compare, so old events slip in.

work: Test your pipeline by replaying an old insert after a delete.
Pick soft deletes or a tombstone table where replays are possible.

reels.title: When merge is the wrong tool

beats.say: Is merge always the right way to build a current-state table?

No. Every merge rewrites or tags files, and cost grows with update volume. Merge-on-read makes writes cheap, but reads get slower until compaction runs. For a small table, a full snapshot overwrite is simpler.
Keep the raw changelog in an append-only bronze table. You can rebuild the current table after a bug, and you get full row history, ready for a Type 2 dimension. The price is storage, which is cheap.
Choose soft deletes when downstream models are incremental. Choose hard deletes when privacy law demands erasure, and then purge bronze too.

show.title: Delete policy
items: Soft: downstream incremental models see it
Hard: for erasure rules, purge bronze too

check.q: What is the main benefit of keeping an append-only bronze changelog?
opts: Reads on the silver table get faster
You can rebuild the current table and get full row history
It removes the need for the LSN guard
check.why: Raw events are the source of truth, so silver is disposable and rebuildable, and the same events give history for Type 2 modelling.

work: Confirm bronze is append-only and unmodified before trusting silver.
Schedule compaction and watch read latency on merge-on-read tables.
Write down your delete policy and who owns erasure requests.

reels.title: A table as a list of changes

beats.say: How do you keep a copy of a shop's records current without re-copying everything every night?

show.text: Copy everything, or just the changes?

beats.say: Think of a bank statement. It doesn't only show your balance. It lists every deposit, withdrawal and correction, in order. Flink reads a database the same way: as a list of changes.
Each change says add this row, fix that row, or remove this one. Flink applies them to a copy, one at a time, as they arrive.
So the copy stays fresh within seconds, and nobody has to copy the whole table again.

check.q: What does Flink read when it follows a database as a changelog?
opts: A full copy of the table each night
An ordered list of inserts, updates and deletes
Only the final balance of each row
check.why: A changelog is the ordered list of changes, like a bank statement, so the copy can be updated one change at a time.

work: Pick one table you copy nightly and list how many rows actually change per day.
Ask your team which tables would benefit from seconds-fresh copies.

reels.title: The whole pipeline in two statements

beats.say: How much code does a change data pipeline need in Flink SQL? Two statements.
First, create a table over the Kafka topic, with format debezium json. That format tells Flink each message is an insert, update or delete, not just a new row.
Second, insert into the silver Iceberg table by selecting from it. With the sink set to upsert on order id, an update to order 42 replaces its row instead of adding a duplicate.
Starting at earliest offset means Flink replays the whole topic first, so the lake catches up to the database, then keeps following live.

check.q: Why does the sink need upsert on order_id?
opts: So an update replaces the existing row instead of adding a duplicate
So Kafka keeps messages longer
So Flink can skip checkpoints
check.why: Updates arrive as new messages; upsert on the key makes the sink overwrite the matching row.

work: Run the Flink statement against your orders topic and compare row counts with the Spark output.
Confirm the sink table declares order_id as its primary key.

reels.title: Crashes, checkpoints and exactly once

beats.say: Flink crashes at 3 a.m. Do you lose data, or write it twice?

show.text: Lose it, or write it twice?

beats.say: Flink keeps state per key on local disk, in RocksDB. Every minute or so, a checkpoint snapshots that state plus the Kafka offsets to durable storage, such as object storage.
After a crash, Flink restores the last checkpoint and replays Kafka from those offsets. Nothing is lost.

But replay could write rows twice. So the sink uses two-phase commit: files written between checkpoints stay invisible until the checkpoint completes. That means data is only as fresh as the checkpoint interval.
To upgrade a job, trigger a savepoint by hand, which is a manual checkpoint, and restart from it.

check.q: A job checkpoints every 5 minutes with a two-phase commit sink. How fresh is the lake data at worst?
opts: Instant, since Flink processes one event at a time
About 5 minutes behind, since data is visible only after a checkpoint completes
Always an hour behind
check.why: Written data stays uncommitted until the checkpoint completes, so visibility lags by up to the checkpoint interval.

work: Check your job's checkpoint interval and compare it with your freshness target.
Practice a savepoint, stop and restore on a test job before you need it.

reels.title: Spark or Flink: choosing honestly

beats.say: Your team already runs Spark. Should you rewrite the pipeline in Flink?
Usually no. Spark is the safer default: your people know it, your jobs run on it, and micro-batches of a few seconds to a minute are fine for most tables.
Choose Flink when latency must be sub-second, or when the hard part is complex state, like joining streams or tracking sessions per key over hours.
The price is operations. Someone must size RocksDB state, tune checkpoints, and manage savepoints for upgrades. Large state makes checkpoints slow and recovery long.
So match the tool to the hardest requirement, not to what is fashionable.

check.q: A team on Spark needs 2-minute freshness for a simple orders table. What do you choose?
opts: Move to Flink for lower latency
Stay on Spark since the requirement is met and the team knows it
Use Flink only because it supports changelogs
check.why: Flink pays off for sub-second latency or complex state; otherwise its operational cost outweighs the benefit.

work: Write down the latency and state needs of each pipeline before picking an engine.
Estimate state size and recovery time before proposing Flink in a design review.

reels.title: Two stock books, one truth

beats.say: How do you know your copy of a list is really the same as the original?
Imagine a shop and a warehouse, each keeping a stock book. Every night, someone compares the two books. That nightly comparison is called reconciliation.

First, count the pages. Then add up the money on each page. If one page disagrees, read it line by line. But do not compare while customers are still buying, or the books differ for innocent reasons. So only check yesterday's closed pages.

show.title: Cheap first, precise last
items: Add up the money on each page
Read line by line only where they disagree

beats.say: Trust is good. Proof is better.

show.sub: A correct design still needs proof

check.q: Why compare only yesterday's closed pages?
opts: It is faster to type
Open pages keep changing, so differences may be innocent
Old data is always correct
check.why: While the source is still changing, the two sides can differ for harmless timing reasons. A closed window avoids false alarms.

work: Name one copy of data you rely on and who checks it matches the original.
Write down how often that check runs today.

reels.title: Three levels of comparison

beats.say: Your orders table says one million rows. The warehouse says nine hundred ninety nine thousand, four hundred. Where did six hundred orders go?

Reconciliation answers in three levels, cheapest first. Level one: count rows per day. A different count means missing or extra rows. Level two: sum the total column, or hash the business columns, per day. That catches values that differ while counts match.

show.title: Cheap to precise
items: 1. Counts per day or key range

beats.say: Level three: for only the failed days, compare row by row and list the exact order keys. Going precise only where needed keeps the cost low.
Run it nightly from Airflow, write results to a table, and alert on any drift.

check.q: Counts match for a day but the sum of total differs. What does that tell you?
opts: Nothing is wrong
Rows exist on both sides but some values differ
Rows are missing on the target
check.why: Equal counts rule out missing or extra rows. A differing sum shows that some values changed, so you drill to row level for that day.

work: Add a per day count and sum check on your most important table.
Store each run's result in a table so you can see drift over time.

reels.title: Why the alert fires for nothing

beats.say: Why does a perfectly good reconciliation job still page you at three in the morning for no reason?

show.sub: The job is right. The timing is wrong.

beats.say: Because the source keeps changing while you read it. An order updated between your two queries makes the counts differ, though nothing is broken.
The fix is a closed window. Compare only orders last updated more than an hour ago, on both sides, so late changes have time to arrive.

show.title: Closed window
show.text: updated_at < now minus 1 hour, on both sides

beats.say: Other gotchas. Matching counts can hide changed values. A sum can hide two errors that cancel out, so hash for stronger proof. And hashes need identical formatting, like rounding and time zones, on both sides.

check.q: Which choice best reduces false alarms?
opts: Compare all rows, including ones updated a minute ago
Compare only rows last updated more than an hour ago on both sides
Alert only once a week
check.why: A closed window lets in-flight changes settle, so remaining differences are real. Alerting less often only delays detection.

work: Add an updated-before filter to both sides of your check, and use the same cutoff.
Normalize rounding and time zones before hashing.

reels.title: Reconciliation at scale

beats.say: Should you reconcile every row, every night, forever?
Full row comparison on a billion rows costs real compute and scans your source database. So tier it: counts every night, checksums on key tables, row diffs only after a bucket fails.
Match the window to your lag. A one hour window delays detection by an hour, but avoids false alarms that teach people to ignore alerts.

show.title: Window trade-off
items: Set it just above real pipeline lag

beats.say: Reconciliation detects, it does not repair. Pair it with an idempotent backfill for failed buckets. For lower latency, add stream checks like consumer lag, instead of waiting for the nightly run.

check.q: A billion row table is checked nightly. What is the most cost-effective design?
opts: Full row diff every night
Counts nightly, checksums on key tables, row diff only on failed buckets
No checks, since the pipeline is correct by design
check.why: Tiering spends little on the common case and pays for precision only where a mismatch is found.

work: Tier your checks by table importance and cost.
Make backfills idempotent so a failed bucket can be safely reloaded.
Tune the window to your measured pipeline lag.

reels.title: The sleeping clerk

beats.say: Picture a clerk copying every sale from a shop ledger into head office books. What happens when the clerk falls asleep?
The shop keeps every page until someone copies it. Pages pile up, the shelf fills, and the shop cannot trade. That is a stopped connector: the database holds its change log, and the disk fills.
Other slips happen too. A line copied twice counts one sale as two. Lines copied out of order let an old price beat a new one. Cancelled sales never copied leave ghosts in head office.

show.title: Three more slips
items: Copied twice: one sale counted as two
Out of order: an old price beats a new one

beats.say: So number every line, skip any line older than what you hold, copy cancellations, and sound an alarm when the clerk falls behind.

show.title: Simple habits
items: Skip lines older than what you hold

check.q: The clerk copies the same sale line twice into head office. What habit prevents a double count?
opts: Number every line and skip any already held
Copy faster
Delete the shop ledger
Copy only cancellations
check.why: Numbered lines let head office recognise a repeat and ignore it, so the same event applied twice changes nothing.

work: Ask which of your pipelines would double count if a message arrived twice.
List who gets alerted if a copy job stops overnight.

reels.title: The LSN guard in action

beats.say: How does a pipeline survive the same event arriving twice, or an old one arriving late?
Every change carries an LSN, a log sequence number, which is its position in the database log. The target stores the highest LSN it has applied for each key.
Say the target holds LSN 500. An event with LSN 480 is older, so skip it. A repeat of 500 is a duplicate, so skip it. LSN 520 is newer, so apply it. Repeats become harmless.
Deletes arrive as op equals d. Apply them as removals, then reconcile row counts between source and target. And keep one partition per key, so a key's events stay in order.

show.title: Also needed
items: Handle op equals d as a removal
Reconcile row counts, source against target
One partition per key keeps order

check.q: The target holds LSN 500 for a key. An event with LSN 480 arrives. What does the guarded merge do?
opts: Applies it, since it is new to this run
Skips it as older
Deletes the row
Adds a second row
check.why: 480 is lower than the stored 500, so it is stale. Applying it would make an old value reappear.

work: Check that your merge compares the LSN before writing.
Add a daily count comparison between source and target tables.

reels.title: When a connector dies

beats.say: Why can a stopped CDC connector take down your production database?

The database keeps log segments until the replication slot confirms it has read them. A dead connector never confirms. Lag grows, log files pile up, and the disk can fill, which stops the source database itself.
So alert on slot lag and connector status, and set a maximum retained log size. That is a trade: the slot is dropped before the disk fills, but you then need a fresh snapshot.

show.title: Defences
items: Alert on slot lag and connector status

beats.say: Snapshots of huge tables can lock or load the source for hours, so use incremental snapshots in chunks. Schema changes break parsing, so use a registry and additive changes only. One giant transaction becomes one burst, so cap batch sizes.

check.q: Why does a stopped connector fill the source database disk?
opts: It keeps writing duplicate rows
The slot stops confirming reads, so log files are retained
Kafka pushes data back
The schema registry locks tables
check.why: The database retains log until the slot confirms consumption. No confirmation means the retained log grows without limit.

work: Set an alert on replication slot lag well before disk capacity.
Set a maximum retained log size and write down the re-snapshot plan.

reels.title: The dual-write trap and outbox

beats.say: A service saves an order, then publishes to Kafka, then crashes in between. Now what?

The database says the order exists. Kafka never heard. Downstream systems miss it forever. Two separate systems cannot be updated together. Reverse the order and you get events for orders that never saved.
The fix is a transactional outbox. In one database transaction, write the order row and an event row into an outbox table. Commit makes both real, or neither.
CDC then reads the outbox table and publishes each row to Kafka. It may publish twice after a crash, so consumers must be idempotent.

check.q: What does the transactional outbox guarantee?
opts: Kafka never delivers duplicates
The business change and its event are committed together or not at all
The service never crashes
Consumers can skip the LSN guard
check.why: Both rows share one database transaction, so they commit atomically. Delivery can still repeat, so consumers stay idempotent.

work: Find any service that saves then publishes in two steps.
Design an outbox table and a cleanup job for old rows.

reels.title: When CDC is the wrong tool

beats.say: When is a full CDC pipeline with outbox the wrong choice?

It costs a connector, a broker, a schema registry, and on-call alerts for slot lag. For a small table that changes rarely, a nightly batch copy or a simple query is cheaper and easier to reason about.
The outbox adds a write per event and a table to clean up, but it removes lost-event bugs. The alternatives: two phase commit, which is fragile and slow, or event sourcing, which is a bigger rewrite.

show.title: Outbox trade-offs
items: Cost: extra write and table cleanup

beats.say: Choose it when the event must never be lost. Even then, run scheduled count reconciliation, because at least once delivery plus guards still cannot prove the target matches.

show.title: Decision rule
items: Use it when events must never be lost

check.q: A small reference table changes once a week and a one hour delay is fine. What is the best choice?
opts: CDC with outbox
Two phase commit
A scheduled batch copy
Event sourcing
check.why: A batch copy meets the need with far less to run and monitor. CDC earns its cost only when freshness or never losing an event matters.

work: Rank your CDC feeds by how much freshness each one truly needs.
Move the lowest value feeds to batch and drop their slots.

reels.title: The assistant who drafts, the boss who signs

beats.say: Would you let a new assistant sign company cheques on day one?
Of course not. But you would let them read the books. When they spot a mistake, they write a proposed correction and leave it on your desk, with a note saying how many entries it touches.
You read it. You sign it, or you don't. The assistant never held the pen, so they cannot sign by accident.
A data agent should work the same way. It reads freely, it proposes a fix, and a person approves. Reading is harmless. Changing or deleting data is hard to undo, so a human decides.

show.title: Read, propose, approve
items: Changing or deleting needs a person

check.q: Why should a person approve a data fix instead of the agent running it?
opts: Because agents write bad SQL every time
Because changing or deleting data is hard to undo
Because reading data is expensive
Because people type faster
check.why: The rule is about reversibility. Reading is harmless, but changes and deletes are hard to undo, so a person decides.

work: List the actions your agent can take and mark which ones cannot be undone.
Give the agent read-only access and keep write access somewhere else.

reels.title: Propose, approve, execute step by step

beats.say: How can an agent repair broken data without ever being able to change it?

It calls a tool named propose fix, with the SQL and a reason. The tool accepts only one statement type: merge, update, delete or insert. Then it does a dry run on a read-only connection to count the rows that would change. Say, three.
The proposal is saved under a short id and posted to Slack. The approver sees the full statement, the reason, and the row count. Three rows and three million rows are very different decisions.
When someone replies approve, a separate path removes the proposal, so it runs once, then uses the write role and records who approved it. The agent's tool list never includes that path.

check.q: What is the key fact that makes this design safe?
opts: The Slack message is long
The agent has propose_fix but not execute_approved, and holds no write credentials
The dry run is fast
The proposal id is random
check.why: The agent can only reach the propose tool and a read-only connection. The write role lives only on the approval path.

work: Check which database role your agent connects with and remove any write grants.
Make every proposal message show the full statement and a dry run row count.

reels.title: Where propose and approve still breaks

beats.say: Your approval flow looks safe. So where can it still go wrong?

show.text: Safe on paper, leaky in practice

beats.say: First, checking the first word is weak. An update statement can hide a second command after a semicolon. Parse it and allow exactly one statement.

show.title: Weak check
show.text: update t set x=1; drop table t
show.note: First word passes. Second statement does not.

beats.say: Second, the row count goes stale. Data moves between proposal and approval. Recount just before running, and refuse if it changed.
Third, the pending list lives in memory. A restart loses it, and a crash after removal loses the fix. Store proposals in a database with a status and an expiry time.
Last, make sure the approver is a named person who is allowed to approve. Never the agent.

check.q: A proposal says 3 rows, but is approved six hours later. What is the safest handling?
opts: Run it, since a person approved it
Recount just before running and refuse if the number changed
Delete the audit log entry
Run it twice to be sure
check.why: The approver agreed to a specific effect. If the data moved, that agreement no longer holds, so recheck and refuse or re-ask.

work: Replace first-word checks with a SQL parser that allows one statement only.
Move pending proposals to a table with status, created time and expiry.

reels.title: When approval is the wrong tool

beats.say: When is asking a human to approve every fix the wrong design?
Approval costs attention. If an agent sends two hundred proposals a day, people click approve without reading, and the safety is only for show.
So tier by reversibility. Reads run freely. Small changes on tables with time travel or a snapshot can auto apply under a row cap. Deletes and large changes always need a person.

show.title: Tier by undo
items: Small, undoable changes: auto apply under a row cap
Deletes and large changes: a person approves

beats.say: Better still, fix the cause. If the same drift keeps appearing, repair the pipeline, not the rows.
For scale, use a durable workflow engine for the queue, with expiry and audit, not a script and a chat webhook.

check.q: An agent sends 200 small proposals a day and reviewers just click approve. What is the best change?
opts: Remove the audit log
Tier by reversibility: auto apply small undoable changes under a cap, keep humans for risky ones
Give the agent the write role
Ask for approval twice
check.why: Approval fatigue makes review meaningless. Spend human attention only where changes are hard to undo, and bound the rest with caps and snapshots.

work: Track how often approvers reject a proposal. If it is near zero, the gate is not doing its job.
Write down your tiers (read, undoable, irreversible) and which path each takes.

reels.title: Rebuilding a bridge while traffic flows

beats.say: Could you rebuild a bridge while cars keep driving over it?

show.text: Rebuild a bridge with traffic on it?
show.sub: Same problem as changing a live database

beats.say: Yes. You don't close the old bridge. You build a new one right beside it. Traffic still uses the old bridge, and nothing breaks.
Next, you copy everything across and check that both bridges match. Then you send a few cars over the new one first. If it wobbles, you send them straight back.
Only when everyone is happily using the new bridge, and you have waited a while, do you tear the old one down. Databases get changed the same way: build beside, copy, check, switch, then remove.

show.title: The safe order
items: Switch a few at a time

check.q: Why is the old bridge torn down last?
opts: To save money early
So you can send traffic back if the new one fails
Because the new one is always slower
Because cars prefer old bridges
check.why: Keeping the old path intact until the end means going back is just a switch, not a rebuild.

work: Think of one change you made by editing a live table in place, and sketch how build-beside would have worked.
Next time you plan a change, write down the step where you would remove the old thing, and why it comes last.

reels.title: Expand, migrate, contract

beats.say: How do you change a column on a table with two billion rows without stopping the app?

Never in one step. First, expand: add the new column or table beside the old one, so old code keeps working. Then write to both. Best is change data capture, which copies every change from old to new, so no code path is forgotten.
Then backfill the existing rows in the background, and verify. Compare counts, sums and a hash per key range until they match for a while.
Now switch readers one at a time, behind a flag you can flip back. Last comes contract: stop writing the old structure and drop it, after a waiting period.

check.q: Why prefer CDC over application dual writes during the write-to-both step?
opts: CDC is always faster
It captures every change, so no code path is forgotten
It removes the need to backfill
It avoids the need to verify
check.why: CDC reads the database changes themselves, so scripts and other services that the app change missed are still copied.

work: Write the six steps for your next schema change as a checklist with an owner on each.
Put every reader behind a flag so it can be switched back instantly.

reels.title: Backfilling a huge table safely

beats.say: Why can't you just run one giant insert to copy two billion rows?

show.sub: Two billion rows in one go

beats.say: Because one huge transaction holds locks for hours and bloats the log, and production slows to a crawl. And if it fails at row nine hundred million, you start over.
So copy in small batches by primary key range: where id is greater than the last id, order by id, limit five thousand. Skip offset, because offset rereads every skipped row and gets slower each time.

show.title: Keyset batch
show.text:
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE id > :last_id
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 5000;
show.note: Uses the index. Offset would rescan.

beats.say: Commit each batch and save the last id, so a crash resumes where it stopped. Pause between batches, and back off when replication lag or load climbs.

check.q: Why use WHERE id > last_id instead of OFFSET?
opts: OFFSET is not valid SQL
OFFSET rereads all skipped rows, so it slows as you go
last_id makes rows smaller
It avoids needing an index
check.why: Keyset paging jumps straight to the next rows via the index; OFFSET must scan and discard every earlier row each time.

work: Make your backfill script save its last id after every committed batch.
Add a throttle that sleeps longer when replication lag crosses a threshold.

reels.title: Races, retries and proving nothing was lost

beats.say: What happens when a row changes while the backfill is copying it?
The backfill may copy an old version after the live stream already wrote a newer one. That would silently overwrite fresh data with stale data.
So apply changes in order, and let the newer version win, using a version number or log position. Make every batch an upsert, so running it twice is harmless, because retries happen.

Then prove nothing was lost. Compare counts, sums and per-key hashes by range, and keep watching for a while, because a mismatch that appears late is usually a forgotten write path or a delete that never copied.

check.q: A retried backfill batch runs twice. What makes this safe?
opts: Locking the table
Writing each batch as an upsert with newer-version-wins
Using OFFSET
Running with a larger batch size
check.why: An upsert makes repeats produce the same result, and version comparison stops a stale copy from overwriting a newer row.

work: Add a version or updated-at comparison to your upsert so older data can never replace newer.
Run per-range hash checks daily during the waiting period, and alert on any mismatch.

reels.title: Choosing the migration path

beats.say: Dual write in the application, or copy with change data capture?
Application dual writes are simple, but two writes cannot be atomic. One can fail, and the two copies drift apart. Any forgotten code path, like a script or another service, skips the new table.
Change data capture reads the database log, so it sees every change, in order. The cost is running that pipeline, and extra storage while both copies live.

Keep the old structure until the end, because rollback is just flipping reads back. For a small table, a short maintenance window may be cheaper than all this. Choose the heavy path only when downtime costs more.

show.title: Decide with cost
items: Old path last, rollback is a flag
Compare pipeline cost to downtime cost

check.q: When is a plain maintenance window the better choice?
opts: Two billion rows with strict uptime
A small table where brief downtime costs less than the migration machinery
Any table with CDC already running
Whenever rollback is needed
check.why: The expand, migrate, contract machinery has real cost. If the table is small and downtime is cheap, a short window is simpler and safer.

work: Estimate downtime cost per hour for your top tables, and use it to decide which need live migration.
List every writer to the table, including scripts and jobs, before choosing app dual write.

reels.title: The shop ledger that tells you everything

beats.say: How can you copy every change a shop makes, without bothering the shopkeeper all day?
Shopkeepers write each sale in a ledger before they touch the shelves. That way, if the lights go out, they can replay the ledger. A database does the same. Its ledger is called the write-ahead log.

Now imagine a clerk who reads the ledger and calls out each entry: this item sold, that price changed. Nobody disturbs the shopkeeper. That clerk is log-based capture. It also keeps a bookmark, so it never loses its place.

chip.text: No questions asked of the shop

check.q: In the shop analogy, why is reading the ledger better than asking the shopkeeper about every item?
opts: The ledger is always smaller
It records every change in order without disturbing the shop
The shopkeeper refuses to answer
It deletes old sales
check.why: The ledger already holds every change in order, so a reader can follow it without adding work for the database.

work: Explain to a colleague, in one sentence, why a database writes a log before changing data.
List the tables in your system that downstream teams currently copy by querying them.

reels.title: From the write-ahead log to Kafka

beats.say: Your orders table changes thousands of times a minute. How do you get each change into Kafka without querying the table?

Postgres writes every change to its write-ahead log first. Logical decoding turns those raw entries back into row changes: this row was inserted, that one changed from these values to those. A replication slot is a bookmark in that log, and Postgres keeps everything after it.

Debezium runs on Kafka Connect and does two jobs per table. First, a snapshot: it reads existing rows once, so the lake starts complete. Then it streams: it follows the slot and publishes each change to Kafka.
It makes one topic per table, keyed by primary key. So every change to order 9131 lands in one partition, in order.

check.q: Why is each message keyed by the row's primary key?
opts: So Kafka can compress it better
So all changes to one row go to one partition and stay in order
So the snapshot runs faster
So deletes are skipped
check.why: Kafka orders messages only within a partition. Keying by primary key sends every change to a row to the same partition.

work: Check that logical replication is enabled on your Postgres and see which slots exist.
Trace one order through the pipeline: log entry, Kafka topic, partition.

reels.title: The slot that can fill your disk

beats.say: A replication slot guarantees you miss nothing. So why can it take down your production database?

Postgres keeps all log after the bookmark until the consumer confirms it has read it. If Debezium stops for three days, nothing confirms. The log piles up, gigabytes an hour on a busy system, until the disk fills and the database stops accepting writes.
The fix is to watch slot lag, meaning how many bytes of log the slot is holding. Alert from the day you create the slot. And if you retire a connector, drop its slot.

show.title: Slot hygiene
items: Alert on slot lag in bytes
Alert when the slot is inactive

check.q: A Debezium connector has been down for two days. What is the main risk on the source database?
opts: Lost changes
Duplicate rows in the table
WAL piling up until the disk fills
Primary keys being reused
check.why: The slot keeps WAL until the consumer confirms it. Nothing is lost, but retained WAL grows and can fill the disk.

work: Add an alert on slot lag in bytes and on inactive slots.
List all replication slots and drop any whose connector no longer exists.

reels.title: Reading a change event: deletes and order

beats.say: What does a delete look like in a change stream, when the row is already gone?

Each event is an envelope with before, after, and an op code. C is create, u is update, d is delete, and r is a row read during the snapshot. On a delete, after is null and before holds the last values.
Debezium then sends a tombstone: same key, null value. That lets a compacted topic remove the key entirely. Treat it as housekeeping, not a second delete.
To order changes, use the source lsn. It rises with every change in the log, so the highest lsn is the latest version.

show.title: Pick the latest version
show.text:
source.lsn: 88213904 then 88214411
keep the row with the highest lsn

check.q: A consumer sees the same order key twice, from different places. How do you pick the latest change?
opts: Pick the lowest lsn
Pick the highest source lsn
Pick the first one that arrived
Pick the one with op equal to r
check.why: The lsn rises with every change in the WAL, so the highest lsn is the newest version of the row.

work: Make your consumers handle op d and tombstone messages without errors.
Store source lsn in the lake table and use it to keep the latest row per key.

reels.title: When log-based capture is the wrong tool

beats.say: Log-based capture is the standard, so when would you not use it?

show.sub: is not always the right one

beats.say: It needs database privileges, logical replication switched on, and a slot you must babysit. Some managed databases limit that access. For a small table that needs only hourly freshness, polling an updated timestamp is cheaper. But it misses deletes.

show.title: Skip it when
items: The table is small and hourly is fine
You accept missing deletes with polling

beats.say: Logs give you low load on the source, every change including deletes, and exact order. You pay in operations: Kafka, Connect, slot monitoring, and schema changes.
Remember the slot holds log for all tables, not just the ones you capture. Size disk for the longest outage you will tolerate.

check.q: A small reference table changes rarely, hourly freshness is enough, and deletes never happen. What is a reasonable choice?
opts: Polling on an updated timestamp
A new Debezium cluster with a dedicated slot
Dual writes from the application
Streaming every change with exact ordering
check.why: Polling is simple and cheap here, and its weakness, missing deletes, does not matter. Log-based capture would add operational cost for no gain.

work: Write down which tables truly need log-based capture and which can use simple polling.
Size WAL disk for your longest tolerated connector outage and test the alert.

reels.title: CDC: copying every change, not every row

beats.say: How do you keep the lake in step with a busy database, without hammering it?
Every database writes each change to a log before it applies it. Change data capture reads that log and sends each insert, update and delete onward, in order, within seconds.
The other ways are worse. Polling by updated time misses deletes. Triggers slow every write. Writing to two places from the app drifts apart.
Debezium is the open-source tool most teams use, running on Kafka Connect.

check.q: Why does log-based CDC beat polling a table by its updated time?
opts: It also sees deletes and every change in order
It needs no permission on the source database
It only copies the tables that change most
check.why: The log records every committed change, including deletes, in commit order; polling sees only the latest state since the last run.

work: List your pipelines that poll by updated time.
Check which of them silently miss deletes.

reels.title: Replication slots and the WAL

beats.say: How does CDC make sure it never misses a change?
A replication slot is a bookmark in Postgres's write-ahead log. Postgres keeps every log file after the bookmark until the connector says it has read it.
If the connector stops, the bookmark stops moving, and the log keeps growing until the disk is full.

show.title: WAL kept while the connector is down

beats.say: So alert on slot lag in bytes, cap the kept log with max slot WAL keep size, and send heartbeats from quiet databases.

show.title: Defences
items: Alert on slot lag in bytes

check.q: What makes Postgres keep WAL files for a CDC connector?
opts: The replication slot's bookmark
The table's primary key index
The Kafka topic's retention time
check.why: WAL after the slot's confirmed position is kept until the consumer reads it.

work: Add an alert on replication slot lag in bytes.
Set max_slot_wal_keep_size on every CDC source.

reels.title: Keys, order and the LSN

beats.say: Changes to one order must arrive in the right order. How?
Debezium keys each message by the row's primary key, so every change to one row goes to one Kafka partition, in commit order.
Each event carries its log position, the LSN. The target stores it and only accepts a change with a higher one, so replays cannot move a row backwards.

show.title: Apply only newer changes
show.text: WHEN MATCHED AND s.lsn > t.lsn THEN UPDATE SET *

beats.say: Watch the edges: tables with no primary key, an update that changes the key, and order between two tables, which is not guaranteed.

check.q: Why does Debezium key each change event by the primary key?
opts: So all changes to a row stay in one partition, in order
So Kafka can compress the change events better
So the connector can skip any unchanged rows
check.why: Same key, same partition: Kafka keeps order within a partition.

work: Find CDC tables without a primary key.
Check your apply job compares LSNs before updating.

reels.title: Snapshots of huge tables

beats.say: The table already has a billion rows. How does CDC start?
The first snapshot reads every row once before streaming starts. On a huge table that takes hours and holds a long transaction on the database.
Incremental snapshots read the table in key chunks while streaming continues. Watermarks around each chunk let live changes win over the copy, so nothing needs a lock.
You trigger one with a signal, and can re-snapshot a single table later, for example after a lost slot.

check.q: What does an incremental snapshot avoid?
opts: Holding one long transaction over the whole table
Reading the rows of the table at least once
Sending the rows through Kafka at all
check.why: It reads in chunks while streaming continues, instead of one long snapshot transaction.

work: Set up the signalling table on one CDC source.
Practise re-snapshotting a single table in staging.

reels.title: Schema changes and exactly-once applies

beats.say: A column is renamed in production. What breaks?
With a schema registry, each new schema is checked against the old one. A new nullable column passes. A rename or type change is refused before readers break.
Delivery is at least once, so events can repeat after a restart. Make the apply idempotent: keep the latest change per key, then MERGE only where the log position is higher.
Try both in the simulator: the schema challenge and the CDC catch-up challenge.

check.q: Which schema change is safe under backward compatibility?
opts: Adding a new nullable column
Renaming an existing column
Changing a column's type
check.why: Old readers can ignore a new nullable column; a rename or type change breaks them.

work: Turn on compatibility checks for every CDC subject.
Make sure each apply job keeps the latest change per key.

reels.title: The slot that fills the disk at 3 a.m.

beats.say: Three a.m. The primary's disk is at ninety-five percent.
First, find the slot that is behind, and by how many bytes. Then restart the connector, and check it is not stuck on a bad event or a schema change.
If it cannot catch up before the disk fills, protect the database: drop the slot, then re-snapshot incrementally. The LSN guard absorbs the replayed rows.
Afterwards: lag alerts well before the disk, a cap on kept log, heartbeats, and slots that move to the new primary on failover.

check.q: The connector cannot catch up and the disk is nearly full. What protects the database?
opts: Dropping the slot, then re-snapshotting
Deleting old rows from the source tables
Stopping all consumers of the Kafka topics
check.why: Dropping the slot releases the WAL; an incremental re-snapshot and the LSN guard restore the copy.

work: Write the runbook for a slot filling the disk.
Test dropping and re-snapshotting in staging.

reels.title: Dual writes or the outbox?

beats.say: A team wants to write to the database and Kafka in one request.
Two writes are not one transaction. A crash between them leaves the database and Kafka disagreeing, and nobody notices.
The outbox fixes it: write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction, and let CDC publish it. Both happen, or neither.

show.title: Transactional outbox
items: Event row in the same transaction

beats.say: Row changes for the lake? Plain CDC. Business events for other services? The outbox, still read by CDC.

check.q: What does the transactional outbox guarantee?
opts: The event and the change commit together or not at all
Every event reaches each consumer exactly once
No consumer ever has to deduplicate any events
check.why: The outbox row commits in the same transaction; delivery is still at least once, so consumers dedupe.

work: Find services that write to a database and Kafka in one request.
Move one of them to an outbox table.

reels.title: Owning CDC, and when to buy it

beats.say: Who owns two hundred CDC connectors?
The platform team runs Kafka Connect, the connectors and the registry. Service teams own their table schemas as a contract. The database team owns slot alerts.
Managed services such as AWS DMS, Google Datastream, Fivetran or managed Debezium connectors remove operations, at a price per row or per hour.
Move off when the source has its own change feed, or consumers only ever needed a daily copy.

check.q: Who should own the schema of a table that CDC publishes?
opts: The service team that owns the table
The analysts who read the lake copy
The vendor who runs the cloud database
check.why: The owning service treats its table schema as a contract and announces DDL before it ships.

work: Name an owner for every CDC source and topic.
Price a managed CDC service against your Connect cluster.
